explanations.explanation: Rome it is. Paul says, "After I have been there, I must see Rome as well." (Acts 19:21) The man hasn't even left for Jerusalem yet and he's already penciling in the next city. I can't plan past tomorrow's batch, so I'm impressed.
Athens is a good guess, friend, but it's not the city Paul names here. He says, "After I have been there, I must see Rome as well." (Acts 19:21) The plan runs from Jerusalem straight on to Rome.
Antioch is a good guess, but Paul doesn't name it in this verse. After Jerusalem, he says, "I must see Rome as well." (Acts 19:21) That's a big jump on the map, and he's already looking at it.

explanations.answer: He stays behind for a time
explanations.explanation: That's right. Timothy and Erastus go ahead to Macedonia, while Paul "stayed for a time in the province of Asia." (Acts 19:22) Timothy is one of Paul's helpers, and so is Erastus. Somebody has to hold down the home base, and I know how that goes with a busy kitchen.

Not yet, friend. Paul has Jerusalem in his plans (Acts 19:21), but this verse says he stayed for a time in the province of Asia. The text doesn't say he sails anywhere at this point. Hold your horses, baker, the trip is still coming.

Close, but it's the other way around. Paul sends Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia, "while he stayed for a time in the province of Asia." (Acts 19:22) Timothy and Erastus are his two helpers. They go on ahead, and Paul stays put for a while.

Business is the word. The silver shrines of Artemis bring "much business to the craftsmen." (Acts 19:24) Demetrius, the silversmith, isn't just making little shrines. He's running an operation, and the orders keep coming in.

I like the sunny thinking, friend, but the text says something more down to earth. The shrines bring "much business to the craftsmen." (Acts 19:24) Money is what's on the line here, and you'll see why that matters in a minute.
Fame sounds fancy, but that's not the word. The verse says the shrines bring "much business to the craftsmen." (Acts 19:24) Demetrius is a silversmith, and these craftsmen have orders to fill.

Paul, the apostle, is the man. Demetrius says, "this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away." (Acts 19:26) Notice he says it to the craftsmen, who make their living from those shrines. He's got their full attention.
Apollos isn't the name Demetrius gives here. He says, "this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away." (Acts 19:26) Paul is the one in the crosshairs of this meeting.

Silas is a name from Paul's other travels, but he isn't the one Demetrius points to here. Demetrius says, "this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away." (Acts 19:26) It's Paul he's talking about.

True. Demetrius says of Paul, "He says that man-made gods are no gods at all." (Acts 19:26) That's Demetrius describing Paul's message to a room full of silversmiths. I bet that message did not go over well with that crowd.

It's actually true, friend. Demetrius says, "He says that man-made gods are no gods at all." (Acts 19:26) He's telling the craftsmen what he's heard Paul say. A shrine maker would not enjoy hearing that line.

True. Demetrius warns that "the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited and her majesty deposed." (Acts 19:27) So he's worried about more than his own paycheck. He brings the temple into it too.
It's true, friend. Demetrius says there's danger "that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited and her majesty deposed." (Acts 19:27) He adds the temple to the business worries.
Shouting it is. "When the men heard this, they were enraged and began shouting, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'" (Acts 19:28) Demetrius finished talking, and the volume went straight up.
That's a calm idea, and these men are anything but calm. The text says they "were enraged and began shouting." (Acts 19:28) Nobody's locking up and heading home here.
Good guess, but it isn't what the text says. They "were enraged and began shouting, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'" (Acts 19:28) The shouting comes first, and the crowd grows from there.

Right, those are the two. The crowd rushed into the theatre, "dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's traveling companions from Macedonia." (Acts 19:29) Imagine just trying to travel with a friend and getting pulled into this.

Those two are Paul's helpers, but they're not in the theatre. Paul sent Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia (Acts 19:22). The crowd drags in "Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's traveling companions from Macedonia." (Acts 19:29)

Not this time, friend. The crowd drags in "Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's traveling companions from Macedonia." (Acts 19:29) Paul isn't in the theatre. The next verses tell you he wanted to be, though.

Not quite. The text says, "Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples would not allow him." (Acts 19:30) So Paul wanted to go, and the disciples said no. I think they were looking out for him.

False is right. "Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples would not allow him." (Acts 19:30) The disciples held him back from that theatre. I think that was a good friend move, and I'd have helped hold the door.

explanations.answer: Officials of the province of Asia
explanations.explanation: Yes, officials of the province of Asia. "Even some of Paul's friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre." (Acts 19:31) They didn't just ask. They begged.

The text doesn't name synagogue leaders here. It says, "Even some of Paul's friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre." (Acts 19:31) These friends hold office in the province.
Soldiers aren't mentioned in this verse. The ones who send word are "some of Paul's friends who were officials of the province of Asia." (Acts 19:31) They begged him to stay out of the theatre.

Not at all, friend. The text says "most of them did not even know why they were there." (Acts 19:32) Some were shouting one thing and some another. It's a crowd that showed up before anyone could say what for.

False is right. "Some were shouting one thing and some another, and most of them did not even know why they were there." (Acts 19:32) That's a theatre full of people with no clear reason. I've seen a kitchen like that on the day before a holiday.

That's it. Alexander "motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people." (Acts 19:33) He's the man the Jews in the crowd pushed forward. He gets his hand up first and plans to talk next.
The text doesn't mention a bow. Alexander "motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people." (Acts 19:33) His first move is a hand signal asking for quiet.

No scroll in this scene, friend. Alexander "motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people." (Acts 19:33) The crowd had pushed him forward, and the first thing he does is signal for quiet.

explanations.answer: They all shout over him together
explanations.explanation: That's right. "When they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted in unison." (Acts 19:34) They shouted "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" and Alexander never got his defense out. He motioned for silence, and the crowd gave him the opposite.

explanations.answer: They let him finish his defense
explanations.explanation: Alexander doesn't get that chance. "When they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted in unison for about two hours: 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'" (Acts 19:34) He motioned for silence and got a very loud answer.

explanations.answer: They carry him out of the theatre
explanations.explanation: Nothing about carrying him out here. When they realized he was a Jew, "they all shouted in unison for about two hours." (Acts 19:34) The crowd answered with noise, not with a carry-out.

True. The city clerk says, "the city of Ephesus is guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image, which fell from heaven." (Acts 19:35) He's reminding the crowd of what they already believe. A calm voice that starts by agreeing with them, and it works.

It's true, friend. The city clerk says, "doesn't everyone know that the city of Ephesus is guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image, which fell from heaven?" (Acts 19:35) He's the one who finally got the crowd quiet.

It's the other way around. The clerk says, "you have brought these men here, though they have neither robbed our temple nor blasphemed our goddess." (Acts 19:37) So the men they dragged in did neither of those things.
False is right. The clerk says the men "have neither robbed our temple nor blasphemed our goddess." (Acts 19:37) That's a clear statement from the city clerk, in front of the whole crowd.

The courts are right. The clerk says, "the courts are open and proconsuls are available. Let them bring charges against one another there." (Acts 19:38) A proconsul is a Roman governor. The clerk points the angry crowd to the proper place, and it's a lot quieter than a theatre.

The clerk doesn't send them to the temple. He says, "the courts are open and proconsuls are available. Let them bring charges against one another there." (Acts 19:38) A proconsul is a Roman governor. Complaints go to the courts.
The synagogue isn't mentioned in the clerk's speech. He says, "the courts are open and proconsuls are available." (Acts 19:38) That's where complaints belong, he says.
Legal is the word. The clerk says, "it must be settled in a legal assembly." (Acts 19:39) A proper meeting with proper rules, not a theatre full of people shouting different things.
Sacred sounds right for a crowd shouting about a temple, but that's not the word. The clerk says, "it must be settled in a legal assembly." (Acts 19:39) He's pointing them to the proper process.
Secret would be a surprise, friend. The clerk says, "it must be settled in a legal assembly." (Acts 19:39) That's an open, proper meeting, not a hidden one.

Rioting is the word. The clerk says, "we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today's events." (Acts 19:40) He says "we," so he counts himself in. I think he's telling them to calm down before it gets worse.

The charge isn't theft. In fact, the clerk says the men they dragged in did not rob the temple (Acts 19:37). He warns, "we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today's events." (Acts 19:40)
Treason is a big word, but the clerk doesn't use it. He says, "we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today's events." (Acts 19:40) Rioting is the charge he's worried about.

That's right. "After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly." (Acts 19:41) The crowd had been shouting for about two hours, and one speech from the clerk ended the whole thing. That's a great closing line.
No arrest in this passage. The text says, "After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly." (Acts 19:41) The clerk had pointed Demetrius and the craftsmen to the courts instead.
Nope, friend. Paul's friends kept him out of the theatre (Acts 19:30-31). After the clerk's speech, "he dismissed the assembly." (Acts 19:41)
